newsitem.title: UK: Gene therapy farther off than people hope - experts.
newsitem.headline: Gene therapy farther off than people hope - experts.

text.p: Gene therapy, which offers the promise of a cure for many diseases, is still in its infancy and faces too many hurdles to offer any immediate hope to patients, experts told a conference on Wednesday.
It was difficult to deliver the new genes into the body and it is still not clear how the immune system responded to efforts to introduced altered DNA, they said.

"It is important to manage expectations about gene therapy," Alan Smith, Senior Vice President of Research at Genzyme Corp, said. "Widespread, pivotal clinical trials are unlikely in the near future."
Julia Dorin of the Medical Research Council's Human Genetics Unit in Edinburgh, agreed. "Too much is wanted too soon," she said. They said they were looking at the next century.
Smith said more work was needed on vectors, which carry the altered genetic material to the target cells. Genzyme is working with a variety of different vectors in its gene therapy trials.
Viruses work because they are programmed to get into a cell and change its DNA anyway. Gene therapists usually alter them in some way so they don't pass on any disease.
But they provoke an immune response, so scientists are working on other vectors like lipids, balls of fat that carry an electric charge that helps them attach to cells.

Helen Hurst of the Imperial Cancer Research Fund told the conference her group also had some success with "naked DNA", which they injected directly into surface nodules that appear on the skin of some breast cancer patients.

"We thought that would be the easiest thing to get through," she said in an interview before the conference. "But I think if gene therapy is really going to be a clinical reality we are going to have to improve the delivery and targeting."
Targeting was a big problem, Smith agreed. "In the case of cystic fibrosis...we are not even sure what the target is and we're not sure we can even get at it," he said.

Cystic fibrosis, the most common fatal recessive genetic disease among whites, is a favoured choice among gene therapists because they know which gene to go for. The fatal disease causes scarring of the lungs and digestive disfunction.

Smith told the conference, sponsored by the Royal Society of Chemistry, that researchers were also still facing obstacles from the body's immune response. He said tinkering with the vectors could help with this problem, as could using other drugs alongside the gene therapy.
In addition, researchers were forced to work with very ill patients in whom it was hard to measure success.
There have been some successes, however. Hurst said although her trials were only in stage I to make sure they did not cause any harm, an effect had been seen on one skin nodule.
"We have seen one of them implode," she said. "Seeing things like that make you think it's worthwhile continuing."

Dorin's group earlier this year reported on a gene delivery trial in which normal cystic fibrosis genes are delivered into patients' noses in drips. The results, although short-lived, have been noticeable.
